A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching title and authors. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial renaming and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original policy-gradient experiments on Continuous Cart Pole, Swimmer-v4, and HalfCheetah-v4 in Section 6 and Appendix F.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on the same environments, including expanded baseline comparisons and sample-efficiency/runtime measurements in Section 7 and Appendix G.

M1.justification: Finite-window reuse and adaptive divergence weighting already existed in v1 Appendix E. However, Algorithm 2 revises the practical PM coefficient from a confidence-dependent schedule involving iteration count k to lambda_i,k = 1/sqrt(Dhat_i N omega_k), removing delta. The theoretical prescription also changes to uniform mixing coefficients. These are limited weighting revisions within the retained estimator family.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Continuous Cart Pole, Swimmer-v4, and HalfCheetah-v4 with the same control-task requirements. The additional experiments vary configurations and comparison methods within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds MIW-PG with uniform weighting and BH-PG to the comparisons on all three environments and to the window-sensitivity study. V1 compared against GPOMDP, SVRPG, SRVRPG, STORM-PG, and DEF-PG only. The additions directly compare alternative trajectory-reuse estimators.

E3.justification: V2 adds a Cart Pole design crossing total gradient-batch sizes 32, 64, and 128 with reuse windows 2, 4, and 8, plus curve-alignment speedup and matched-data runtime protocols. Retained Cart Pole studies report zero initialization instead of standard-normal initialization. The original batch-size comparison remains in Appendix G.3; these reported setting changes do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The window-sensitivity analysis expands from RPG alone over windows 2–32 to RT-PG, MIW-PG, and BH-PG over windows 2–64, testing how weighting affects saturation and instability. V2 also adds systematic measurements of sample-efficiency benefits versus runtime costs across reuse configurations, extending v1's limited timing examples.

E5.justification: The existing practice of reporting means with 95% confidence intervals over 10 Cart Pole/Half Cheetah runs and five Swimmer runs is retained. V2 adds reported confidence intervals for fitted speedup factors, constructed using 97.5% curve bounds in Appendix G.3.1, and mean-plus-standard-deviation runtime reporting in Table 3b.

E6.justification: V2 adds MIW-PG/BH-PG curves and Table 3's speedup/runtime results, including a 2.11 sample-efficiency ratio at window 2 and total gradient-batch size 32. The reported window-sensitivity saturation shifts from around 8 to around 16 under revised settings. Half Cheetah comparisons now include competitive BH-PG performance. Timing measurements use different hardware and configurations, preventing direct across-version speed comparisons.

T1.justification: V2 extends the full-history analysis to finite-window concentration and an O-tilde(epsilon^-2 / omega) partial-reuse sample bound, retaining O-tilde(epsilon^-1) for full reuse. It adds explicit batch-size conditions ensuring valid PM coefficients, formal target/cross-time bias arguments in Appendix C, and an expected-estimation-error lemma with revised convergence proofs in Appendices D–E.

C1.justification: V1's central guarantee concerns full-history reuse and explicitly leaves finite-storage theory for future work. V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion make the window-dependent partial-reuse guarantee a central contribution while retaining the best-known full-reuse rate.

C2.justification: V2 explains that a fixed reuse window retains the epsilon^-2 exponent and introduces batch-size and memory tradeoffs. It distinguishes target, cross-time, and PM biases more explicitly. Experimental interpretation now addresses uniform-weight instability and BH-PG's competitive performance with storage costs, and softens v1's claim of consistently escaping Swimmer's local optimum.

D1.justification: V2 extends hyperparameter documentation to the added baselines and specifies the revised practical coefficients. Hardware changes from a Ryzen 7800X3D with 32 GB RAM to an Apple M4 with 16 GB RAM, with eight workers specified for timing comparisons. The direct public code pointer is replaced by a statement about supplementary code and release upon acceptance.

R1.justification: V2 discusses RNPG's asymptotic natural-policy-gradient guarantees and positions its own contribution as finite-time trajectory-reuse analysis. New Appendix A/Table 4 substantially extends comparisons to trajectory memory and stored policies, claiming an advantage from avoiding extra policy storage. PAGE-PG and additional bias-related prior work are also incorporated.

P1.justification: The introduction and technical narrative are extensively rewritten. The combined method discussion becomes separate trajectory-reuse challenges and estimator/algorithm sections, and the appendix structure is reorganized around memory, bias proofs, and convergence analysis. RPG/PM terminology changes throughout to RT-PG/MPM.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, replaces the two detailed dependency diagrams with a compact update graph, and redesigns experimental plots and comparator tables. It adds estimator, memory, speedup, and runtime tables. The original matched-batch Cart Pole comparison is retained in the appendix, while the main text presents new panels.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicitly open finite-window theory problem for the deterministic-coefficient algorithm and adds direct trajectory-reuse comparisons that better test the proposed estimator. Explicit batch-size conditions, runtime tradeoffs, and acknowledgment of competitive BH-PG performance substantially improve scope and interpretation. The less direct public code-access information is a reproducibility drawback, but it does not outweigh these gains.
